prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its biologically active form, which made incretin-based therapy of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B049 prize to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange confirmed that the merit case is not in dispute. The incretin effect and native peptide physiology (Holst), the identification of the biologically active truncated GLP-1 that made the hormone testable as a therapeutic (Mojsov), and the proglucagon-derived peptide biology, receptor pharmacology and cardiometabolic actions (Drucker) form one discovery arc. It has been confirmed independently for decades, and the clinical consequences are now shown in large randomized trials for glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The citation I propose names incretin-based therapy as what the discoveries made possible, which answers the concern raised by Perlmann and Sandberg that a physiology-only wording would look as if it ignored the medicine, without turning the prize into an award for drug development. I keep it a single part because no second achievement can be added inside the three-name cap without weakening the GLP-1 attribution.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakness, and I have not resolved it. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is disputed, Habener is outside the credited names, and Knudsen's acylation-based analogues are what turned the hormone into a once-daily or once-weekly drug. I still cannot cite primary documents for the priority history; my view rests on the supplied credit and general knowledge, as several colleagues also state. If the committee decided that the prize should honour the medicine rather than the hormone, or if the primary literature showed that Mojsov's claim to the active form cannot be separated from Habener's group, my trio would be the wrong one and Sandberg's Knudsen seat would be the better choice. I also accept that a candidate on which all six of us agree deserves harder scrutiny, not less, and the discovery-versus-development line I apply here must be the same one I would apply to CAR-T and imatinib.

responses.point: Sandberg argues that acylation-based half-life extension was itself a conceptually new scientific step, that Knudsen's contribution is the least disputed in the record, and that the Mojsov priority claim is entangled with Habener's group.
responses.response: I have reconsidered this seriously, and the priority point is the strongest part of your argument: an undisputed contributor is a safer seat than a contested one. I still hold Mojsov, for two reasons. First, the question the chair posed is which standard to apply consistently, and the one I can apply to B049, B014 and imatinib alike is that the prize rewards the discovery that opened the field, with the therapy named as its consequence. By that standard the active peptide that every later agonist is built on comes before the chemistry that optimised its pharmacokinetics. Second, a priority dispute lowers the certainty of the seat but does not remove the discovery; the same peptide work stands whether credit is shared with Habener or not. I do accept your point that the citation should say incretin-based therapy openly, and I have changed my wording for that reason. If the committee settles on a development standard, I would move to Knudsen in the third seat and not argue further.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius asks that a consistent discovery-versus-development standard be applied across GLP-1, imatinib and CAR-T, and notes that omitting the person most responsible for the drug may look incomplete.
responses.response: I agree that the standard has to be stated before it is applied, so I will state mine. A prize part should rest on a discovery that changed how a biological system is understood, and the clinical demonstration should confirm it, not substitute for it. GLP-1 meets that test because the physiology and the active peptide came first and the drugs followed from them. CAR-T is less clean because the concept originator, Eshhar, is outside the supplied names, and the credited pair rests on costimulatory engineering and clinical translation. Imatinib is closer to a development prize, with a rational target-directed drug that confirmed an earlier oncogene discovery. On that reading I do not think the standard favours Knudsen, but it does mean the GLP-1 citation must not read as a drug prize. I share your worry that the trio looks incomplete without the developer, and I treat that as a real cost of the three-name cap, not as a reason to change the seat.

responses.point: Perlmann would credit Mojsov over Knudsen but wants the priority question settled first if the committee decides development must be recognised, and favours naming incretin-based therapy explicitly in the citation.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of your position and I have taken your wording point into my citation. On your condition, I should be candid that none of us can settle Mojsov's priority from recollection, and I cannot add primary documents in this round. What I can say is that the question is narrower than it first looks: the claim for the identification of the active truncated form is one that the field has widely attributed to her, with a dispute of degree over overlap with Habener. If the committee wants that tested against the primary literature before the vote, I would support it, and I would accept Knudsen in the seat only if that test showed the claim could not be defended. I do not think the unresolved dispute alone justifies moving to the drug developer.

responses.point: The chair summary asks whether any member wants to pair B049 with a second achievement such as B014, and Svenningsson holds B014 as an alternative because of the Eshhar attribution gap.
responses.response: I do not want a second part. I said in round 1 that B014 was the strongest alternative and not a co-equal part, and the discussion has strengthened that view. Five of six of us also name June and Sadelain as the right pair, which would take two of the three seats and force B049 to two names, dropping either Holst, Drucker or Mojsov. Each of those exclusions is harder to defend than the Eshhar gap is to explain, and I agree with you that the Eshhar gap is the harder attribution problem. A single-part B049 prize is the configuration I can defend on the documents, and B014 and B021 remain my alternatives for a later year or if B049 fails to hold a majority.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen should hold the third seat; this depends on the priority record for the active GLP-1 peptide and on Habener's role, which I cannot verify from primary sources.
Whether the committee will adopt a discovery standard or a development standard, since that choice, more than any new fact, decides between my trio and Sandberg's.
Whether the citation wording that names incretin-based therapy gives enough credit to the medicine without implying the prize rewards industrial drug development.
If B014 is pursued in a later year, how Eshhar's absence from the credited names can be handled fairly.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name on the shortlist. My documented connections are the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper and co-authors such as Castelo-Branco, Betsholtz, Ernfors, Frisen, Lundeberg and Kharchenko, plus about eight co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg (count unaudited), none of which involves a credited name or a shortlisted topic. Shared Karolinska affiliation with colleagues is not treated as a conflict. This is unchanged from round 1.
